evidence: Cic. N.D. 3.83: aestāte grave esse aureum amiculum, hieme frīgidum (Lewis & Short)
Hor. S. 1.9.21: cum gravius dorsō subiit onus
terms.comment: The opposite is levis, light. Heavy sleep is gravis somnus (Plin. NH 9.42); heavy rain, magnī imbrēs (Traupman 136). Serious, important is gravis too (see major, important).
Of weight it is rare (Lucr., Ov.); far more often it means severely, seriously, deeply: graviter aegrōtāre, to be seriously ill; graviter ferre, to take something hard (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: dēmittō auriculās, ut inīquae mentis asellus, cum gravius dorsō subiit onus
phrases.english: I let my ears droop, like a sulky donkey when a heavier load has been put on his back

phrases.latin: vēnālēs umerō fascēs portābat in urbem: inde domum cervīce levis, gravis aere redībat
phrases.english: he carried bundles on his shoulder to sell in town, and came home light in the neck and heavy with money
